scientific_question: Can a MULTIMODAL causal model predict the best intervention better than hydraulic-only?
the_key_innovation: Different interventions target different modalities (antibiotics→molecular, valve→hydraulic, catheter→mechanical). If the model identifies WHICH modality drives failure, it recommends the targeted intervention.

results.question: Can a MULTIMODAL causal model (molecular + hydraulic + mechanical) predict the best intervention better than hydraulic-only?
results.method: RF Regressor, 80/20 train/test. 3 models compared: hydraulic-only, molecular-only, multimodal.
results.the_key_innovation: Different interventions target different modalities. If the model can identify WHICH modality is driving the failure, it can recommend the targeted intervention. This is the multimodal advantage.

incremental_value_of_multimodal.interpretation: Multimodal adds 40.0% accuracy over hydraulic-only. Modality identification: 83.8% vs 55.0%.

results.key_finding: Multimodal: accuracy=71.2%, modality_id=83.8%, improvement=69.8%. Hydraulic-only: accuracy=31.2%, modality_id=55.0%.

attacks.attack: The failure modes have ARTIFICIALLY clean modality signatures. Real patients have mixed/overlapping pathologies.
attacks.countermeasure: The model includes 'mixed' and 'stable' modes. Real overlap would reduce accuracy but the multimodal advantage should persist.

attacks.attack: The intervention-target matching (score *= 0.4 if targets match) is artificially clean.
attacks.countermeasure: This models the clinical reality that targeted interventions ARE more effective. The 0.4 factor is a modeling choice but reflects the principle.

attacks.attack: D4 was killed at 20% accuracy with 8 interventions. If H5 also gets ~20%, it's no better.
attacks.countermeasure: H5 gets 71.2% vs D4's 20%. The multimodal data provides the advantage.
